HIPÓTESIS FINAL (respuesta a "How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?")

**EN (versión para el entregable):** In the NLSY79 1989 cross-section (n = 12,686, ages 24–32), age is negatively associated with the probability of dissaving — i.e. of having taken more money out of savings than was put in (DISSAVED = 1, base rate 23.6%). In the main model (LPM with HC1-robust SEs; DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE_2 + INCOME + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC), each additional year of age is associated with a **0.76 percentage-point lower probability of DISSAVED** (coefficient −0.0076, SE 0.0016, p ≈ 1e−5), and the quadratic AGE_2 term is negative (−0.145 pp per year², p = 0.059), implying a decline that is steepest at older ages. The relationship is **approximately monotone decreasing and essentially linear within 24–32**: comparing age 32 with age 24, the fitted probability falls from 25.1% to 18.7%, a drop of **−6.4 pp (95% CI −9.0 to −3.9), i.e. about a 26% relative reduction** (logit: −6.3 pp, CI −8.7 to −3.8; flexible age-dummy model: −7.2 pp, CI −11.9 to −2.4; observed raw gap: −7.3 pp). Flexible age dummies (24…32, reference 24) show no significant differences from age 24 up to age 29 (−2.3 to +0.5 pp, all p > 0.17) but significantly lower dissaving at ages 30 (−5.3 pp, p = 0.002), 31 (−4.0 pp, p = 0.019) and 32 (−7.2 pp, p = 0.003); the block contrast 30–32 vs 24–29 is −4.5 pp (CI −6.4 to −2.7). The joint age effect is highly significant (F = 4.12, p = 6e−5), but there is **no evidence of a U or inverted-U**: free age dummies do not improve on a single linear age term (LR = 11.1, 7 df, p = 0.13) and the fitted quadratic's turning point (age ≈ 25) sits at the edge of the observed window. The pattern is not an artefact of the DISSAVED dichotomy: a 3-state multinomial shows that with age "savings increased" rises from 30% to 55%, "unchanged/no savings" falls from 44% to 26%, and "dissaved" falls from 25% to 19%. Interpretation (not demonstrated here): consistent with time-preference — younger adults discount the future more and are more likely to draw down savings — but as a single cross-section these coefficients mix age, cohort and 1989 period effects and must not be read as the causal effect of ageing.

**ES:** A mayor edad en el corte de 1989, menor probabilidad de retirar más dinero del ahorro del que se aporta: ≈ **−0.8 puntos porcentuales por año** (−0.0076, SE 0.0016, p < 1e−5), con curvatura negativa marginal (AGE_2: −0.145 pp/año², p = 0.059). Caída **aproximadamente monótona y lineal** dentro de 24–32: de 25.1% a los 24 a 18.7% a los 32 (**−6.4 pp**, IC 95% −9.0 a −3.9; ~−26% relativo). Las dummies de edad indican que el descenso se concentra a partir de los 30, sin soporte para ninguna "U" ni "U invertida".

EVIDENCIA CLAVE
1. M1 (titular, LPM/HC1, pp por unidad): AGED −0.765 (SE 0.162, p 1e−5); AGED2 −0.145 (p 0.059); INCOME +0.0126 (p 0.0004); FEMALE +3.35; BLACK +3.40; HISPANIC +1.65 (ns). R² = 0.0058.
2. Jerarquía: solo-edad −0.774 pp/año; M1 −0.765; M2 (+BMI) −0.773; log-ingreso −0.845. Estable ante controles.
3. Logit vs LPM vs probit (M1): logit AGED −0.0436 (p < 1e−5), AGED2 −0.0087 (p 0.048); probit −0.0254 / −0.0050. Probabilidades previstas por edad coinciden con LPM en ≤0.35 pp (p.ej. 24: 25.1 LPM vs 25.1 logit; 32: 18.7 vs 18.8). Mismo signo y magnitud.
4. Efecto marginal de +1 año (LPM M1): +0.35 pp a los 24 (ns) → −1.10 a los 29 → −1.96 pp a los 32 (p 0.003); negativo y significativo desde ~27.
5. Forma: dummies F conjunta = 4.12 (p 6.3e−5) pero LR dummies vs edad lineal = 11.14 (7 df, p 0.133) → relación lineal decreciente suficiente.
6. Multinomial 3 estados: AGED −0.141 (same vs save-more) y −0.113 (dissave vs save-more), ambos p < 1e−3.
7. Descriptivo: tasa observada 25.5, 24.1, 25.8, 26.3, 24.1, 23.3, 20.2, 21.6, 18.2 % para 24…32 (Spearman edad–tasa = −0.78, p = 0.013).

LIMITACIONES: asociación transversal (edad = edad + cohorte + período 1989); ventana estrecha 24–32 con solo 379 casos a los 32 (poco poder en los extremos, no extrapolable); INCOME contiene artefactos (31.2% de filas con el valor idéntico 47.279, probablemente imputación; 167 top-codeadas en 1,057.45; 131 en 0) por lo que su control es frágil — de ahí la sensibilidad con log-ingreso; sin pesos muestrales de NLSY79, las tasas no son representativas; poder bajo para forma funcional (R² ≈ 0.006; la edad explica solo una fracción pequeña de la variación individual del desahorro); no se observan riqueza, deuda, estado civil ni ingresos esperados, de modo que el mecanismo de preferencia temporal es interpretativo y no queda separado de otras explicaciones (ciclo vital de ingresos, liquidez,Composition de la muestra).

payload.hypothesis: Age is negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in (DISSAVED). In the NLSY79 1989 cross-section (n=12,686, ages 24-32, base rate 23.6%), the main model DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE_2 + INCOME + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC (linear probability model, HC1-robust) gives -0.0076 per year of age, i.e. about 0.8 percentage points lower probability of dissaving per additional year (SE 0.0016, p ~ 1e-5), with a negative quadratic term AGE_2 (-0.145 pp per year^2, p = 0.059) so the decline steepens with age. The relation is approximately monotone decreasing and essentially linear inside the observed 24-32 window: predicted probability falls from 25.1% at age 24 to 18.7% at age 32, a drop of -6.4 percentage points (95% CI -9.0 to -3.9; logit -6.3 pp; flexible age dummies -7.2 pp; raw gap -7.3 pp), roughly a 26% relative reduction. Flexible age dummies show no significant departure from age 24 up to age 29 but significantly lower dissaving at 30-32 (-4.0 to -7.2 pp), and they do not improve on a single linear age term (LR = 11.1 on 7 df, p = 0.13), so no U-shaped or inverted-U pattern is supported. Robust to adding BMI, to using log income, and to logit/probit instead of the LPM. A three-state check (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) shows that with age the 'savings increased' share rises from 30% to 55% while 'unchanged' falls from 44% to 26% and 'dissaved' falls from 25% to 19%, confirming a real shift toward positive saving rather than an artefact of the dichotomy. Interpretation, not a demonstrated finding: this is consistent with age differences in time preference (younger adults discount the future more and draw down savings more often). Because it is a single cross-section in 1989, the estimate mixes age, cohort and period effects and should not be read as the causal effect of ageing; income is partly imputed (31% of rows share one value, plus top-coded values) and no survey weights are available, so magnitudes are sample-specific.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspection of data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 x 9, no missing, AGE_2 = AGE^2, DISSAVED and SAMESAVE mutually exclusive, overall P(DISSAVED)=0.2355). 2) Descriptives by age year (rates of dissaving / unchanged / saved more, income medians). 3) Hierarchical LPM (HC1) and logit (HC1) models: raw age+age^2; M1 = age+age^2+INCOME+GENDER+BLACK+HISPANIC (main); M2 = M1+BMI; M1 with log income. SAMESAVE deliberately excluded as a regressor. 4) Functional form: LPM with age dummies 25-32 (ref 24) plus M1 controls, joint F test, LR test of dummies vs a single linear age term, AGE^2 Wald test, block contrast 30-32 vs 24-29. 5) Average predicted probabilities at each age with delta-method SEs (LPM, logit, probit) and marginal effect of +1 year of age. 6) Contrast 32 vs 24 in percentage points with 95% CIs across all estimators. 7) Three-state multinomial logit (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) as an interpretation check. 8) Figure: observed rates with 95% CIs plus fitted M1 and crude age-only curves (SVG, generated without matplotlib). All steps in analysis/nls_dissave_age_analysis.py, executed end to end (exit 0); outputs in analysis/results_log.txt and the CSV tables.
payload.main_model: LPM (HC1): DISSAVED ~ AGE_c + AGE_c^2 + INCOME + FEMALE + BLACK + HISPANIC, n=12686, R2=0.0058
payload.shape_conclusion: approximately monotone decreasing, no significant departure from linear (LR p=0.13); decline concentrated at ages 30-32
